questions.stem: Which conditions define a feasible s-t flow?
choices: Capacity at each edge and conservation at every vertex including s and t
Capacity at each edge and conservation at every vertex except s and t
Each vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree
questions.explanation: Capacity (0 <= f(e) <= c(e)) on edges plus conservation at internal vertices only. s produces; t consumes.

questions.stem: The capacity of an s-t cut (A, B) is:
choices: Sum of capacities of all edges between A and B in either direction
Sum of capacities of edges from A to B only
Number of edges from A to B
Max capacity edge crossing the cut
questions.explanation: Only A->B edges count; B->A edges are ignored in cut capacity.

questions.stem: The Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem states:
choices: Max flow value = min cut capacity
Max flow value <= min cut capacity
Max flow value > min cut capacity
questions.explanation: Strong duality: the optimal flow value equals the optimal cut capacity.

questions.stem: An augmenting path in the residual graph G_f is:
choices: A simple s-t path along which flow can be increased
The shortest path from s to t in G
questions.explanation: Augmenting paths in G_f have positive residual capacity along the whole path and let you push more flow.

questions.stem: Backward edges in the residual graph represent:
choices: The ability to undo (cancel) existing flow along an edge
questions.explanation: Each f(e) > 0 induces a residual backward edge (v, u) of capacity f(e), allowing the algorithm to reroute previously committed flow.

questions.stem: What is the running time of Ford-Fulkerson with integer capacities and max flow value F?
questions.explanation: Each augmentation increases the flow by >= 1; each takes O(m) to find. F augmentations give O(mF).

questions.stem: Why is Ford-Fulkerson's O(mF) bound NOT polynomial in input size?
choices: Because F can be exponential in the bit-length of the capacities
Because the graph has many edges
It is polynomial — the question is wrong
questions.explanation: F is bounded by a value, but values take only O(log F) bits. O(mF) is pseudo-polynomial.

questions.stem: Once max flow has been computed, how do you find the min cut?
choices: Run the algorithm again with reversed edges
Set A = vertices reachable from s in G_f; B = V \ A
questions.explanation: On termination, the reachable-from-s set in the residual graph gives a saturated min cut with cap(A, B) = |f|.

questions.stem: Integrality of max flow with integer capacities means:
questions.explanation: With integer capacities, every augmentation pushes an integer bottleneck, so the final flow is integer. Essential for combinatorial reductions.

questions.stem: Edmonds-Karp differs from Ford-Fulkerson by:
choices: Always choosing the shortest augmenting path (BFS)
questions.explanation: BFS gives the shortest augmenting path. Its analysis bounds the number of augmentations by O(mn), so total time O(m^2 n).

questions.stem: Weak duality for max flow / min cut says:
choices: |f| <= cap(A, B) for every feasible flow f and every s-t cut (A, B)
questions.explanation: Weak duality: any feasible flow is bounded above by any feasible cut. Strong duality says optima coincide.

questions.stem: Which three statements are equivalent for a flow f?
choices: f is max | no augmenting path in G_f | exists cut with cap = |f|
f is min | f saturates s | t is unreachable
f integer | path exists | capacities positive
G is acyclic | f = 0 | min cut = 0
questions.explanation: The MFMC theorem proves these three are equivalent. (1->2 trivially, 2->3 via reachability, 3->1 by weak duality.)

questions.stem: Why does the flow-value lemma matter?
choices: It establishes that for ANY cut, the net flow across equals the source-side surplus, enabling weak duality and the min-cut characterisation
It is used to compute residual graphs
questions.explanation: The lemma is the bridge: |f| can be measured at any cut. Together with capacity it gives |f| <= cap(A, B).

questions.stem: If c(e) = 0 for some edge e, what does it mean for the flow?
choices: e contributes to capacity of every cut
questions.explanation: Capacity constraint 0 <= f(e) <= c(e) forces f(e) = 0 when c(e) = 0.

questions.stem: The number of augmenting paths in Edmonds-Karp is bounded by:
questions.explanation: Each augmenting-path length is monotone non-decreasing and bounded by n; careful counting gives O(mn) augmentations. Combined with O(m) BFS this gives O(m^2 n).

questions.stem: Why must Ford-Fulkerson use the residual graph rather than the original graph for path search?
choices: To allow flow rerouting via backward edges, which is essential for optimality
questions.explanation: Without backward edges some max flows are unreachable: a wrong early augmentation can block subsequent improvements. Backward edges let the algorithm undo.

questions.stem: If a flow has |f| equal to the capacity of some s-t cut, the flow is:
questions.explanation: Weak duality bounds every flow by every cut capacity; equality is achievable only at optimum. So |f| = cap(A, B) certifies max-flow.

questions.stem: A network where every edge has unit capacity 1 will have:
choices: Max flow at most min(n, m)
An integer max flow value bounded by the number of edge-disjoint s-t paths
questions.explanation: With unit capacities the max-flow value equals the maximum number of edge-disjoint s-t paths (Menger). Foundation of Week 7's reductions.

questions.stem: In Ford-Fulkerson, the bottleneck of an augmenting path P is:
choices: The maximum residual capacity on P
The minimum residual capacity on P
The total residual capacity of P
questions.explanation: Bottleneck is the smallest residual capacity along P; this is how much you can push without violating capacity.

questions.stem: Why does s-t cut capacity exclude B->A edges?
choices: Because flow from B to A reduces, not increases, |f|; including those edges would not bound it properly
Because such edges do not exist
questions.explanation: Net flow out of A is the A->B flow minus the B->A flow. Counting A->B capacity alone gives the right upper bound on flow.

questions.stem: If max flow value is 7 and min cut capacity is 7, what does this confirm?
questions.explanation: Strong duality: equality of flow and cut certifies both at optimum. This is the standard way to verify a max-flow answer on an exam.

questions.stem: Ford-Fulkerson with irrational capacities may:
choices: Fail to terminate on adversarial examples
questions.explanation: Famous example: with bad augmenting-path choice and irrational capacities, FF can keep augmenting forever. Edmonds-Karp avoids this.

questions.stem: What is the value of an s-t flow?
choices: Sum of capacities of all edges
Net flow out of s (equivalently, net flow into t)
Sum of flow on all edges
Sum of f(e) on edges out of t
questions.explanation: |f| is measured at s (or equivalently at t by conservation).

questions.stem: Which is FALSE about residual graphs?
choices: G_f has the same vertex set as G
G_f has at most twice as many edges as G
G_f has residual capacities derived from f and c
questions.explanation: G_f is directed: forward edges represent slack, backward edges represent cancellation, and they are distinct.

questions.stem: Which best characterises why Ford-Fulkerson's correctness proof yields the Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem 'for free'?
choices: The termination argument constructs a cut with capacity equal to the final flow value
questions.explanation: On termination the reachable-from-s set yields a cut whose capacity matches the flow value, simultaneously certifying max flow and min cut.
